content: Toxicodendron diversilobum, also known as Western Poison-oak or Pacific Poison-oak, is a plant species found exclusively along the Pacific Coast of the United States and Canada. It is particularly abundant in this region and is the dominant species of its genus. A closely related species, Atlantic Poison-oak (Toxicodendron pubescens), is found on the Atlantic Coast. Appearance Western Poison-oak exhibits significant variability in its growth patterns and leaf morphology. In open, sunny areas, it grows as a dense shrub, while in shaded environments, it can climb as a vine. Similar to Poison Ivy, it propagates through creeping rootstocks or seeds. Its leaves are trifoliate, meaning they are divided into three leaflets, each measuring 3.5 to 10 centimeters in length. The edges of the leaflets may be scalloped, toothed, or lobed, resembling the leaves of true oak trees, though Poison-oak leaves are typically glossier. In spring, the leaves are bright green or bronze when they first emerge. During summer, they transition to yellow-green or reddish hues, and in autumn, they turn vivid shades of red or pink. The plant produces white flowers in the spring, which, if fertilized, develop into greenish-white or tan berries. Toxicodendron diversilobum is a deciduous plant, shedding its leaves in winter. During this time, its stems are bare, occasionally displaying clusters of berries. Poison-oak stems can sometimes be identified by black marks where sap has oozed and dried. Habitat Western Poison-oak is restricted to the Pacific Coast, ranging from southern Canada to the Baja California peninsula. It is one of the most widespread woody shrubs in California and can also grow as a climbing vine, particularly on tree trunks. It thrives in oak woodlands and Douglas-fir forests and is commonly found in damp, shaded areas near streams or waterfalls. For example, trails leading to waterfalls along California’s coast are often home to this plant. In northern California, it can be seen climbing the trunks of Coast Redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) along the Avenue of the Giants. Toxin The leaves and twigs of Western Poison-oak are coated with urushiol, an oil that triggers allergic reactions in most individuals. For those affected, urushiol causes a highly irritating rash. Severe cases may require treatment with corticosteroids to alleviate rashes and intense itching. These can progress to blistering, and in severe cases, the blisters may ooze clear fluid. Once urushiol binds to the skin, it cannot be washed off, although prompt washing immediately after contact can remove the oil before it binds. After urushiol is removed, the rash cannot spread through contact with the affected area or by scratching. The fluid from blisters does not spread the toxin. However, scratching can break the skin, increasing the risk of secondary bacterial infections. The blisters and oozing result from fluid leakage through gaps in blood vessels. Cooling the skin can constrict these vessels and reduce fluid leakage. Inhalation of smoke from burning Poison-oak can cause the rash to develop on the lining of the lungs, leading to severe pain and potentially life-threatening respiratory complications. Ingestion of the plant can damage the digestive tract, airways, kidneys, or other organs. Urushiol oil remains active for years, meaning contact with dead leaves or vines can still provoke a reaction. Additionally, the oil can be transferred to other objects, such as pet fur, and subsequently cause a rash upon skin contact. Note on Name Hyphenation The hyphenated form Poison-oak is used to clarify that the plant is not a true oak, just as Poison-ivy is not a true ivy.
